messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Arthur was sixty years old when he finally sought help, but the event that brought him here happened decades ago, during a deployment overseas. He had been part of a supply convoy moving through a congested urban area when a roadside bomb detonated. The memory itself was a terrifying blur of noise, blinding light, and the acrid smell of burning fuel and dust. He remembered the sickening lurch of the vehicle, the shouts, and then a deafening silence. When he came to, he was outside the truck, miraculously thrown clear, but his co-driver and two others in the back were gone. He had survived, untouched physically, while they had perished.

Since then, the world had never felt safe to Arthur. He had come to believe, deep in his bones, that the world was a dangerous place, a belief reinforced by every news report of violence or accident. What truly haunted him, though, was the memory of the ambush itself. When he remembered the event, the same primal terror he felt at the time would flood through him, chilling him to the core. But alongside that terror was an intense, crushing guilt. He felt an overwhelming sense of guilt for surviving when others did not, a burden that had settled heavy on his shoulders and never left. He would often replay fragments of the event, trying to make sense of it, but it was like trying to grasp smoke. He knew what had happened, he could tell you the basic facts, but he was unable to find words to describe the visceral experience, the chaos, the emotional reality of it. It was just a knot of sensation and horror, inarticulate and stifling.

Over the years, Arthur developed a series of strategies to cope with these overwhelming feelings. He meticulously avoided going to or near any place that resembled the narrow, dusty streets where the ambush occurred. This meant staying away from certain industrial zones in his own city, and even changing his route to work at the warehouse if it meant skirting a particular type of building or alleyway that felt too similar. He also found himself avoiding wearing clothes that reminded him of his time in uniform. His wardrobe now consisted almost entirely of muted tones and casual wear; anything resembling military fatigues, or even the sturdy, olive-green work jackets many of his colleagues wore, was meticulously avoided and quickly discarded if acquired. Most profoundly, he tried to avoid thinking about the event altogether. When a fragment of the memory would intrude, a flash of fire or a sudden noise, he would immediately try to distract himself, diving into paperwork at the warehouse, focusing intensely on stacking boxes, or losing himself in television at home.

This constant effort to avoid had slowly but surely reshaped Arthur's life. He used to be a gregarious man, quick with a joke and always ready to lend a hand. Now, he felt like he didn't know himself anymore. The man he was before the deployment, the confident and outgoing Arthur, seemed to have vanished, replaced by a cautious, quiet individual. His partner, Susan, had noticed the change years ago, but recently it had worsened. His difficulty communicating the depth of his internal struggles, coupled with his increasing withdrawal, had created a distance between them. At the warehouse, he preferred solitary tasks, often taking longer routes to avoid specific areas that felt too enclosed or noisy, leading to a noticeable drop in his overall efficiency. He’d turned down opportunities for promotion to a supervisory role because it would require more interaction and less control over his environment, something he wasn't willing to risk.

Lately, the intrusive memories had grown more frequent, the terror and guilt more intense, despite his best efforts to push them away. Susan, worried by his increasing isolation and the haunted look in his eyes, had gently but firmly encouraged him to seek help. Arthur arrived at the clinic feeling a profound weariness, still certain the world was a dangerous place, but desperate for some relief from the incessant internal battle that had defined his life for so long. He didn't know if he could ever truly find himself again, or if the past would forever dictate his present.
